title: King Over All Israel: Jerusalem Taken
summary: The tribes of Israel come to Hebron, make a covenant with David, and anoint him king over all Israel. David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Zion, makes it his capital, the City of David, and grows greater because the LORD is with him. Hiram of Tyre builds him a palace, more sons are born to him, and David twice defeats the Philistines in the Valley of Rephaim after inquiring of the LORD.
story: This is the turning point of David's life. The boy anointed in secret by Samuel (1 Samuel 16), who waited through years of danger and refused to take the throne by force, is now anointed by the whole nation. The long division that followed Saul's death is over. David immediately does two things that shape the rest of Israel's history. He takes Jerusalem, a city that belonged to no tribe, and makes it the capital of a united kingdom, and he breaks the Philistine power that had crushed Saul. The chapter reads like a summary of a successful reign, and it is arranged by theme rather than strict chronology. It prepares directly for chapter 6, where David brings the ark to Jerusalem, and chapter 7, where God promises David an everlasting house.
historical:
David's reign over all Israel began around 1003 BC, after seven and a half years at Hebron (the dates are approximate). Jerusalem was a Canaanite city held by the Jebusites; Israel had failed to take it permanently in the days of Joshua and the judges (Joshua 15:63, Judges 1:21). It sat on a narrow ridge, now called the City of David, south of the later Temple Mount, protected by steep valleys on three sides and supplied by the Gihon spring. Its position between Judah and the northern tribes made it an ideal neutral capital. The supporting terraces (the Millo) were probably the stone terraces built on the slope to support buildings above; archaeologists have uncovered a massive stepped stone structure on the eastern slope of the City of David, though its date and relation to David are debated.

The water shaft David mentions (verse 8) has long been linked with a vertical shaft found by Charles Warren in 1867, known as Warren's Shaft, but later excavations suggest that shaft was not accessible in David's time, and the Hebrew word itself is uncertain. Hiram king of Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city on the coast, supplied cedar and craftsmen; since Hiram was also Solomon's ally (1 Kings 5), many scholars think his help with the palace came later in David's reign and is placed here by theme. The Philistine battles in the Valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem, may have come before the capture of the city, when the Philistines first heard that David ruled all Israel.
cultural:
The tribes' words, your own flesh and blood (literally your bone and your flesh), are the language of kinship, the same idiom Laban uses of his nephew Jacob (Genesis 29:14). The northern tribes are acknowledging that David is family, not a foreign conqueror. Kingship was sealed by covenant before the LORD, with obligations on king and people alike, and by anointing. Taking a city and naming it after oneself, the City of David, marked it as the king's personal possession by conquest, independent of any tribal territory.

The Jebusites' taunt, that even the blind and lame could keep David out, mocked his army's chances against their walls. David turns the insult back on them, and the saying that grew from it is obscure; it may reflect a later rule restricting access to the palace or temple. Kings in the ancient world often took more wives and concubines as their power grew, many of them to seal alliances. Carrying off an enemy's idols after battle was a way of showing that the victor's god had defeated theirs; in 1 Samuel 4 the Philistines had captured Israel's ark, and here Israel carries off the Philistine gods. The balsam trees are an uncertain species, and the sound of marching in their tops signaled the LORD going out ahead of his army.
literary: The chapter is an arrangement of short units, each showing David's kingdom established: the covenant at Hebron, the summary of his reign, the capture of Jerusalem, the palace and family, and the two Philistine victories. Two statements stand at its center and interpret the rest: “David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him” (verse 10), and David's recognition that the LORD had exalted his kingdom “for the sake of His people Israel” (verse 12). The kingdom is God's gift, given for the people's good. The two Philistine battles are carefully contrasted: in the first the LORD tells David to go up, and in the second to circle around, showing that David must inquire each time rather than assume. The name Baal-perazim, meaning lord of breaking through, plays on David's words that the LORD has burst out against his enemies.

outline.t: All Israel anoints David king at Hebron
Sons born to David in Jerusalem

doctrines.note: David's kingdom is established by God and for God's people. The tribes remember the LORD's words that David would shepherd Israel, and David understands that he was exalted for the sake of the people. Kingship in Scripture is service under God, not ownership of a nation.

David makes a covenant with the elders before the LORD. The king does not rule by conquest of his own people but by a sworn relationship with them under God, a principle that limited royal power in Israel even when kings ignored it.

The narrator's explanation for David's success is simple: the LORD God of Hosts was with him. Military skill, political alliances, and a strong capital all matter in the story, but the book attributes the outcome to God's presence.

words.note: Raah, to shepherd or pasture. The LORD's word was that David would shepherd his people Israel. In the ancient Near East kings were often called shepherds, but in Israel the image carried special weight because David had been a literal shepherd and because the LORD himself is Israel's shepherd (Psalm 23, 80:1). The king's calling is to feed, guide, and protect, not to exploit.

Nagid, leader or ruler. It is used of Saul and David when they are designated by God (1 Samuel 9:16, 13:14), and many scholars think it stresses the ruler's appointment by the LORD rather than his royal status. David is God's appointed leader before he is Israel's king.

Tsiyyon, Zion. First named here as the Jebusite fortress, Zion becomes the name for the City of David, then for the temple mount, then for Jerusalem as a whole and for God's people. In the Psalms and prophets Zion is the city where the LORD dwells and reigns, and in the New Testament the heavenly Zion is the city of the living God (Hebrews 12:22).

Parats, to break through or burst out. David names the place Baal-perazim because the LORD burst out against his enemies like a flood. The same verb returns in chapter 6, when the LORD bursts out against Uzzah, a reminder that the power that breaks through for Israel is holy and not to be handled lightly.

christ: Several threads here run forward to Jesus. The people remember God's word that David would shepherd Israel; the prophets later promised a coming shepherd from David's line (Ezekiel 34:23-24), and Jesus called himself the good shepherd (John 10:11). Matthew 2:6 quotes Micah's prophecy of a ruler from Bethlehem and completes it with words drawn from this very verse, that he will shepherd God's people Israel, tying the birth of Jesus to David's shepherd kingship. Zion, first taken by David here, becomes the city where the Messiah was expected to reign; Jesus enters Jerusalem as its king (Matthew 21:5), and Hebrews speaks of believers coming to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem. Two of the sons listed here, Solomon and Nathan, are the lines through which the genealogies of Matthew and Luke trace Jesus's descent from David (Matthew 1:6, Luke 3:31).

hard.q: What does David's statement about the blind and the lame mean, and does it show contempt for disabled people?
hard.a: Verse 8 is one of the hardest in Samuel to translate. The Jebusites mocked David by saying even the blind and lame could hold him off, and David turns their taunt around, calling the Jebusite defenders the lame and blind who are despised by David. On this reading, the phrase refers to the enemy soldiers, not to disabled people in general. The saying that follows, that the blind and the lame will never enter the palace (literally the house), may be a later proverb growing from the event; some connect it with rules about access to the temple (compare Leviticus 21:17-23 for priests). Interpreters differ, and the Hebrew is uncertain. What is clear from the wider story is that David later shows lavish kindness to the lame Mephibosheth, seating him at the king's table (2 Samuel 9), and that Jesus welcomed the blind and lame in the temple and healed them (Matthew 21:14). Whatever this proverb meant, Scripture does not treat disability as a reason for exclusion from God's grace.

questions: David understood that God had exalted him for the sake of the people. How would your use of influence change if you saw it as given for others' good?
David asked God before each battle, even after victory, and received different instructions each time. Where do you assume you already know what to do because it worked before?
The tribes came to David saying they were his own flesh and blood. What helps divided people rediscover a shared identity?
